subject: nlp
title: Practice bank: Lecture 3 (Text classification and CNNs)
description: New quiz-style practice questions on text classification and CNNs, with tf-idf, softmax and cross-entropy, CNN output-shape, parameter-count and receptive-field calculations. Written for exam revision from the Lecture 3 slides and the tutorial. Not from the lecturer: the answers are unofficial.
negativeMarkingNote: The real Moodle quiz uses negative marking on MCQ questions: picking all right and wrong answers on a question results in a mark of 0.

questions.question: Match each example to its classification type.

pairs.prompt: Which of 20 news topics an article is about
Choosing all the hashtags that fit a tweet

questions.explanation: Multi-label: several labels can be correct at once, so each label gets its own yes/no decision (sigmoid), unlike a single softmax.

questions.question: Which output layer suits a multi-label problem (several labels can be correct)?
choices: A sigmoid per label with binary cross-entropy for each
One softmax over all labels with multiclass cross-entropy
A single sigmoid
An argmax with no probabilities
questions.explanation: A softmax forces the labels to compete and sum to 1, which suits exactly one correct label. Contrast next-token prediction (L5), where one softmax and multiclass CE is right.

questions.question:
A classifier's linear layer outputs scores $(2,0.5,-1)$ for classes (pos, neu, neg). The true class is "neu".
(a) $P(neu)$ after the softmax. (b) The cross-entropy loss (natural log). (c) The loss if the true class were "pos".
questions.explanation: With a one-hot target, cross-entropy is $-\log p(\text{correct class})$: low when the model is confident and right, high when it is confident and wrong.

questions.question: Which statements about the final linear layer + softmax of a neural classifier are true?
choices: It is logistic regression on the feature vector $h$
Each class $k$ has a weight vector $w_k$, and its score is $w_k \cdot h + b_k$
Training makes text vectors point in the direction of their class vectors
It maps from $K$ classes back to $d$ features
questions.explanation: It maps $d \to K$. The class weight vectors are "vector representations of classes" (slide 37).

questions.question: Which statements describe the "features + classifier" view?
choices: A feature extractor turns the text into a vector $h$; a classifier turns $h$ into a probability distribution over classes
In classical methods, a human designs the features (e.g. bag of words, n-grams)
In neural methods, the network learns which features matter
Neural features are always easier to interpret than hand-crafted ones
questions.explanation: Interpretability is a weakness of learned features (Quiz 1 Q23).

questions.question:
Three documents: D1 "the cat sat on the mat", D2 "the dog sat", D3 "a cat and a dog". Use $\text{tf-idf}(w, d) = N(w, d) \times \ln\frac{|D|}{|\{d \in D: w \in d\}|}$ (natural log).
(a) tf-idf(the, D1)  (b) tf-idf(cat, D1)  (c) tf-idf(mat, D1)  (d) tf-idf(a, D3)
questions.explanation: A word that appears in every document gets idf $\ln 1 = 0$. tf-idf weights are one way to weight a bag of embeddings (slide 47). The slide does not fix the log base; state the one you use.

questions.question: A word appears in every document of the corpus. What is its idf?
choices: The number of documents
Undefined
questions.explanation: $\log(|D|/|D|) = \log 1 = 0$, so it gets no weight however often it appears.

questions.concept: Bag of embeddings and weighted BOE
questions.question:
A 3-word text has embeddings $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(3,3)$.
(a)–(b) The bag of embeddings (sum). (c)–(d) The weighted BOE with weights $(0.5,0.25,0.25)$.
questions.explanation: Word order is lost in both: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" give the same vector.

questions.concept: Convolution as a linear layer on windows
questions.question: True or False: A convolution with $m$ filters and kernel size $k$ over $d$-dimensional embeddings is a linear layer from $k \cdot d$ to $m$, applied to every window.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 78: concatenate the $k$ vectors in the window (size $k \cdot d$) and multiply by a $(k \cdot d) \times m$ matrix.

questions.concept: CNN output shapes, stride and padding
questions.question:
A 1D convolution runs over a sentence of 12 tokens with 100-dimensional embeddings, using 64 filters of width 3.
Give the number of output positions for (a) stride 1, no padding, (b) stride 1 with 1 padding token on each side, (c) stride 2, no padding. (d) How many channels does each output position have?
questions.solution:
Output length $= \lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1$.
(a) $12 - 3 + 1 = 10$. (b) $12 + 2 - 3 + 1 = 12$ (padding keeps the length, like the slide's <pad> tokens). (c) $\lfloor 9/2 \rfloor + 1 = 5$. (d) One channel per filter: 64.

questions.question: Same layer: 64 filters of width 3 over 100-dimensional embeddings. (a) Weights per filter. (b) Total parameters including one bias per filter. (c) Total if the kernel width is 5 instead.
questions.explanation: The count does not depend on the sentence length: the same weights are reused at every position (parameter sharing).

questions.question:
A sentence classifier (as in "CNNs for Sentence Classification") uses three convolutions with kernel sizes 2, 3, 4, each with 100 filters, over 300-dimensional embeddings, then max-over-time pooling and concatenation, then a linear layer to 5 classes.
(a) Convolution parameters (with biases). (b) Size of the concatenated vector $h$. (c) Parameters of the final linear layer (with biases).

questions.concept: Several kernel sizes, stacking and receptive field
questions.question:
How many input tokens does one output of the last layer see (its receptive field)?
(a) Two stacked width-3 convolutions, stride 1.
(b) Three stacked width-3 convolutions, stride 1.
(c) Width-3 convolution, then width-2 pooling with stride 2, then a width-3 convolution (all other strides 1).
questions.solution:
$r = 1 + \sum_l (k_l - 1)\prod_{i<l} s_i$.
(a) $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$. (b) $1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7$. (c) $1 + 2 + 1 + 2 \times 2 = 8$: pooling with stride doubles how far the next layer reaches.
questions.explanation: Stacking blocks lets later layers see longer phrases; a larger kernel also grows the receptive field (Quiz 1 Q10).

questions.question: Which statements about invariance and equivariance are true?
choices: Convolution is translation equivariant: shifting the input shifts the feature map
Global max pooling over the feature map makes the result translation invariant
A CNN classifier with global pooling still depends on the order of words inside each window
Global pooling makes the model care exactly where in the text a phrase occurs
questions.explanation: "We don't care where the cat is, we care that it is somewhere."

questions.question: Why is global pooling needed before the linear layer in a CNN text classifier?
choices: It turns a variable-length sequence of feature vectors into one fixed-size vector
It adds non-linearity
It increases the number of filters
It makes the model recurrent
questions.explanation: The final block is always global pooling: "you need it to get a single vector".

questions.concept: CNN output shapes, stride and padding
questions.question: A width-5 convolution (stride 1, 2 padding tokens on each side) runs over 20 tokens with 50 filters, followed by local max pooling of size 2 with stride 2. What is the output shape (positions × channels)?
questions.explanation: Convolution: $(20 + 4 - 5)/1 + 1 = 20$ positions × 50 channels. Pooling 2 with stride 2 halves the positions: 10 × 50. Pooling never changes the number of channels.
